**LA PAZ, Bolivia** — Former Bolivian President Evo Morales has renewed his defense of a controversial 2008 decision to expel the U.S. ambassador from the country, while also drawing attention to remarks he made at the United Nations regarding climate change and Earth Day.

Morales, who served as Bolivia's president from 2006 to 2019, expelled then-U.S. Ambassador Philip Goldberg in September 2008, accusing him of conspiring with opposition groups to destabilize his government. The move came amid escalating tensions between La Paz and Washington and was followed by the U.S. expelling Bolivia's ambassador in a tit-for-tat response.

Speaking recently to supporters and media, Morales reiterated that the expulsion was justified, characterizing it as a necessary defense of Bolivian sovereignty against what he described as foreign interference in the country's internal affairs.

"We will not allow any foreign power to conspire against the will of our people," Morales said, according to accounts of his remarks. He has long maintained that the decision reflected his broader political philosophy of resisting what he views as U.S. imperialism in Latin America.

The former president's comments come as he continues to position himself as a global voice on indigenous rights and environmental issues. Morales has previously addressed the United Nations on Earth Day, using the platform to call for greater international action on climate change and to advocate for the rights of "Mother Earth" — a concept central to his political ideology and Bolivia's 2010 Law of Mother Earth.

In his UN remarks, Morales has historically emphasized the disproportionate impact of climate change on developing nations and indigenous communities, while criticizing industrialized countries for what he calls insufficient action to curb greenhouse gas emissions.

Morales remains a polarizing figure both within Bolivia and internationally. Supporters credit him with reducing poverty and asserting Bolivian autonomy on the world stage, while critics point to allegations of authoritarian overreach during his tenure, including a disputed 2019 election that led to his resignation amid widespread protests.

CNN has reached out to the U.S. State Department for comment on Morales' renewed remarks regarding the 2008 expulsion.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

Morales has consistently framed these actions as necessary defenses against what he characterizes as U.S. interventionism in Latin America, often linking this critique to his broader condemnation of capitalist and imperialist structures he blames for environmental degradation.
